lesson.title: Coils and Sheets: The Backbone Finds a Rhythm
lesson.summary: Secondary structure describes the regular, repeating local shapes, alpha helices and beta pleated sheets, that a polypeptide backbone folds into as hydrogen bonds form between the backbone's own carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens.
lesson.body:
Once a polypeptide chain exists, it does not stay stretched out in a straight line. Short, local stretches of the backbone settle into regular, repeating patterns, and these patterns are what we call secondary structure. Secondary structure only involves the repeating atoms of the polypeptide backbone itself, the nitrogen, alpha carbon, and carbonyl carbon of each amino acid, not the side chains sticking off of it. The two most common secondary structures, the alpha helix and the beta pleated sheet, are both held in place by hydrogen bonds, specifically hydrogen bonds between the carbonyl oxygen of one amino acid and the amide hydrogen of another amino acid further along the same backbone.

In an alpha helix, the polypeptide backbone coils into a right-handed spiral, and a hydrogen bond forms between the carbonyl oxygen of one amino acid and the amide hydrogen of the amino acid four positions further along the chain. That regular spacing produces a tight, uniform coil with about 3.6 amino acids per full turn, while the side chains of each amino acid point outward, away from the coil's core. Alpha helices are the dominant structure in keratin, the fibrous protein that makes up hair, nails, and the outer layer of skin, where bundles of helices twist together to form tough, stretch-resistant fibers.

In a beta pleated sheet, the backbone instead extends into a mostly straight strand, called a beta strand, and hydrogen bonds form not within one strand but between neighboring strands lying side by side. Those strands can run in the same direction, called a parallel sheet, or in opposite directions, called an antiparallel sheet, and the resulting structure has a pleated, zigzag appearance when viewed edge on, with side chains alternating above and below the plane of the sheet. Silk fibroin, the protein spiders and silkworms spin into fiber, is built largely from stacked antiparallel beta sheets, which is part of why silk fibers resist stretching so well.

Not every amino acid fits equally well into these patterns. Proline has an unusual, ring shaped side chain that loops back and bonds to its own backbone nitrogen, which both removes the hydrogen needed for normal hydrogen bonding and locks the backbone at a fixed angle, so proline frequently interrupts or bends an alpha helix or beta strand rather than extending it. Glycine, at the opposite extreme, has only a single hydrogen atom as its side chain, giving the backbone extra flexibility that makes glycine common in tight turns that connect one secondary structure element to the next.

None of this folding would be possible without the properties of the peptide bond covered earlier. Because the peptide bond itself is rigid and planar, the polypeptide backbone can only rotate at the bonds on either side of each alpha carbon, and it is exactly this restricted, repeatable rotation that allows the same hydrogen bonding pattern to repeat itself over and over, producing the uniform coils of an alpha helix or the regular pleats of a beta sheet.
